The curved path a thrown or launched object follows through the air, set by its launch speed, angle, gravity and air resistance.
Two coils wound around a shared iron core that use changing magnetism to raise or lower AC voltage. It only works with alternating current, which is a big reason the power grid uses AC.
A semiconductor switch or amplifier with three leads, where a small signal on one lead controls a much larger current through the other two. Billions of them make up every computer chip.
A siege engine that throws a shot from a sling on a long lever arm, powered by a falling counterweight (or, in early versions, people pulling ropes).
A symbol or named value that can represent different numbers, measurements, or data.
The electrical push between two points in a circuit, measured in volts (V). More voltage pushes more current through the same resistance.
A graph of a signal over time, usually voltage up the side and time along the bottom, like the trace on an oscilloscope.
The minimum energy needed to free an electron from a material.
A highly reactive metal in group 1 of the periodic table, such as lithium, sodium, or potassium.
The height of a wave — how far it swings from its resting middle line. For sound, bigger amplitude means louder.
A negative ion, formed when an atom gains electrons. Nonmetals usually form anions, like Cl⁻ or O²⁻.
The smallest unit of an element that still has that element’s chemical properties.
The number of protons in an atom’s nucleus; it identifies which element the atom is.
A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up by the reaction.
The terminal where conventional current leaves a diode or LED. On the symbol it is the bar; on a real LED it is the short leg beside the flat edge.
A positive ion, formed when an atom loses electrons. Metals usually form cations, like Na⁺ or Mg²⁺.
An attraction that holds atoms or ions together by sharing or transferring electrons.
An attraction that holds atoms or ions together, created by the transfer or sharing of outer electrons.
Shorthand that lists the elements in a substance and how many of each: in C₆H₁₂O₆ the subscripts mean 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen, 6 oxygen.
A number that multiplies a variable or quantity, such as 3 in 3x.
A pure substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, like H₂O (always 2 H to 1 O). Its properties are different from the elements that made it.
A bond in which two atoms share a pair of electrons, usually between two nonmetals.
A repeating 3D pattern of particles. In an ionic compound, each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge in every direction.
Two atoms sharing two pairs of electrons (O=C=O). A triple bond shares three pairs, like N≡N. More shared pairs means a shorter, stronger bond.
A model showing the regions around a nucleus where an electron is likely to be found.
How strongly an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself. A big difference between two atoms points toward an ionic or very polar bond.
A pure substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons.
A pure substance made of only one kind of atom, such as oxygen (O) or sodium (Na). It cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical reactions.
The capacity to cause change or do work, such as moving, heating, or lighting something.

terms.definition: A cycle where a system measures the result of what it just did and uses that measurement to decide what to do next, then repeats.
A push or pull that can change an object’s motion or shape.
A rule that assigns exactly one output to each allowed input.
The job a part does. The function of a structure in a living thing, a machine, or a design is what it is for and how it helps the whole work.
The lowest frequency in a musical sound — the rate at which the whole wave pattern repeats. It sets the pitch you hear.
The branch of mathematics that studies shapes, sizes, positions, and spaces.
A vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in a group often behave similarly because they have related valence-electron patterns.
The time required for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay.
A reactive nonmetal in group 17, such as fluorine, chlorine, bromine, or iodine.
A sine-wave component of a sound at a whole-number multiple (2×, 3×, 4×…) of the fundamental frequency. The mix of harmonics gives an instrument its timbre.
A strong attraction between molecules (not inside one) where a hydrogen on N, O, or F is drawn to a lone pair on a nearby molecule. It keeps water liquid at room temperature.
A testable explanation or prediction based on observations and prior knowledge.
An atom or group of atoms with an electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
The attraction between oppositely charged ions after electrons transfer, usually from a metal to a nonmetal.
A compound built from positive and negative ions stacked in a lattice, like NaCl. Usually brittle solids with high melting points that conduct electricity when melted or dissolved.
A form of an element whose atoms have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.
The energy of motion, ½mv². Double the speed and the kinetic energy is four times as big.

terms.definition: A diagram that shows valence electrons as dots around element symbols, with shared pairs drawn as lines between atoms.
A pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom and is not shared in a bond. Lone pairs push bonds apart and bend molecules like water.
An element with a mixture of metallic and nonmetallic properties, often useful as a semiconductor.
Two or more substances physically mixed but not chemically bonded, like salt water or air. The parts keep their own properties and can be separated physically.
A compound made of separate molecules held together by covalent bonds, like water or carbon dioxide. Usually lower melting points; often liquids or gases at room temperature.
The 3D shape of a molecule (linear, bent, trigonal, tetrahedral…), set by how electron pairs spread out as far apart as possible.
A separate group of atoms held together by covalent bonds, like one H₂O. A molecule can be an element (O₂) or a compound (CO₂).
Two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds as a single unit.
A solid where every atom is covalently bonded to its neighbors in one giant continuous structure, like diamond or quartz (SiO₂). Very hard, very high melting.
An element in group 18 with a filled outer electron shell, making it unusually unreactive.
A covalent bond where electrons are shared evenly, as between two identical atoms in Cl₂ or N₂.
The pattern that many atoms tend to bond until they have eight electrons in their outer shell, like a noble gas. Hydrogen is satisfied with two.
A horizontal row of the periodic table. Atomic number increases by one from left to right.
A chart that orders elements by atomic number and lines up repeating patterns in their chemical properties.
The process plants, algae, and some bacteria use to turn light energy, water, and carbon dioxide into sugars.
A covalent bond where the electrons are shared unequally, giving one end a slight negative charge and the other a slight positive charge, as in H–Cl.
A charged group of covalently bonded atoms that acts as one unit in a compound, like carbonate (CO₃²⁻) in chalk or hydroxide (OH⁻) in lye.
Energy stored because of position or shape: a lifted weight, a stretched band, a twisted rope. It can turn into motion.
A positively charged particle in an atom’s nucleus. The number of protons determines the element.
An early model built to test an idea, reveal problems, and guide improvements.
Creative works whose copyright has run out (or never existed). Anyone may copy, perform and change them.
A comparison of two quantities by division, often written with a colon or as a fraction.
How readily a substance undergoes a chemical change when it meets other substances.
A chart of a signal’s ingredients: each frequency it contains and how much of it there is.
The small lowered number in a chemical formula that tells how many atoms of the element before it are present. No subscript means one.
The curved path a thrown or launched object follows through the air, set by its launch speed, angle, gravity and air resistance.
The smallest repeating three-dimensional pattern that can build an entire crystal lattice.
An electron in an atom’s outermost occupied shell that helps determine bonding and reactivity.
An electron in an atom's outermost shell. These are the electrons that take part in bonding.
A symbol or named value that can represent different numbers, measurements, or data.
A method that uses the way X-rays scatter from a material to determine how its atoms are arranged.
A precise sequence of steps for solving a problem or completing a task.
An organic molecule with amino and carboxyl groups; α-amino acids are the monomers used to build proteins.
The variety of living things in an area, including differences among species, genes, and ecosystems.
Light made by living things through a chemical reaction, usually involving a molecule called luciferin. Common in the deep sea.
The end with the free carboxyl group; conventionally written on the right.
A three-nucleotide mRNA word that specifies an amino acid or translation stop signal.
A number in an ordered set that identifies a point’s position on a grid or in space.
Loss of a protein’s native folding and activity without necessarily breaking its peptide backbone.
A community of living things interacting with one another and with their physical environment.

A cycle where a system measures the result of what it just did and uses that measurement to decide what to do next, then repeats.
A push or pull that can change an object’s motion or shape.
The job a part does. The function of a structure in a living thing, a machine, or a design is what it is for and how it helps the whole work.
The branch of mathematics that studies shapes, sizes, positions, and spaces.
A picture of how two quantities are related, with one quantity on each axis and points or a line showing their values.
The natural home of a plant or animal, like an ocean, forest, desert, or arctic.
A testable explanation or prediction based on observations and prior knowledge.

terms.definition: What happens when two waves overlap: where crests meet crests they add up and get stronger, and where crests meet troughs they cancel out.
The stages a living thing passes through as it is born (or hatches), grows, and changes.
Something that breathes, eats, grows, responds, and can make more of its kind.
A figure of speech that describes one thing as another to suggest a meaningful comparison.
Two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds as a single unit.
The end of a peptide with the free amino group; conventionally written on the left.
The things a living thing must have to survive: water, air, food, and space.
Something that does not breathe, eat, grow on its own, or reproduce.
The young that a living thing produces — puppies, chicks, and seedlings are all offspring.
The planar covalent amide link, –CO–NH–, joining one residue to the next.
The process plants, algae, and some bacteria use to turn light energy, water, and carbon dioxide into sugars.
A comparison of two quantities by division, often written with a colon or as a fraction.
An amino acid after it has joined a chain and lost the atoms used to form peptide bonds.
The latitude lines at 23.4°N (Cancer) and 23.4°S (Capricorn): the farthest north and south the Sun is ever straight overhead. Their latitude equals Earth's tilt.

terms.definition: A symbol or named value that can represent different numbers, measurements, or data.
A molecule carrying positive and negative formal charges at the same time.
The darker strip of sky between the primary and secondary rainbows, where no once- or twice-reflected sunlight can leave the drops toward the viewer.
The exit angle where rays from a wide band of a raindrop bunch together. Light piles up there, making the bright bow about 42° from the antisolar point.
The point in the sky directly opposite the Sun from the viewer, marked by the shadow of the viewer's head. Rainbows are circles centered on it.
The point in an orbit where a planet is farthest from the Sun. Earth reaches it around July 4, at about 152.1 million km.
The latitude line at about 66.6°N (66.6°S for the Antarctic Circle). Beyond it there is at least one day of 24-hour sun and one of 24-hour night each year.
The angle between a planet's spin axis and a line straight up from its orbit. Earth's is about 23.4°, and it is the cause of the seasons.
An imaginary line through Earth's center, from the North Pole to the South Pole, that Earth spins around once a day.
The process that moves carbon from the ocean surface into the deep sea as sinking particles and migrating animals, keeping it out of the atmosphere.
Light made by living things through a chemical reaction, usually involving a molecule called luciferin. Common in the deep sea.
At a constant temperature, a gas’s volume shrinks as its pressure rises: double the pressure, half the volume.
A large volcanic depression formed by collapse after magma withdrawal.
A system for counting days using repeating cycles: lunar (Moon), solar (seasons), or lunisolar (both).
Making food from chemical energy (such as hydrogen sulfide from vents) instead of sunlight. Microbes at hydrothermal vents and cold seeps do this.
The splitting of white light into colors because each color (wavelength) refracts by a slightly different amount.
The gathering of water in oceans, lakes, rivers, and soil. Collected water is stored until it evaporates again or infiltrates into the ground.
The process by which water vapor cools and changes back into liquid water droplets. This forms clouds and fog.
A number in an ordered set that identifies a point’s position on a grid or in space.
Camouflage in which an animal glows on its underside to match the faint light from above, hiding its silhouette from predators below.
A body of magma that pushes into a volcano without emerging at the surface.
A mixture of abundant solid crystals and interconnected molten rock in a magmatic system.
Erupted material volume expressed as compact rock without pore spaces; abbreviated DRE.
The process by which water vapor turns directly into ice without becoming liquid first — it's how frost forms.
The daily trip many sea animals make — rising toward the surface to feed at night and sinking back to deep, dark water by day. By mass, it is the largest migration on Earth.
A sheet-shaped intrusion that cuts across surrounding rock layers.
One of two moments each year (about March 20 and September 22) when the Sun is straight over the Equator and day and night are nearly equal everywhere.
The process by which soil and rock particles are worn away and moved elsewhere by gravity, or by a moving transport agent – wind, water, or ice.
The process by which liquid water turns into water vapor and rises into the atmosphere. Heat from the Sun powers this process.
Separation of dissolved gas from magma as conditions change, often during pressure decrease.
A broad, nearly white rainbow made by tiny fog droplets. The drops are so small that each color spreads across several degrees, and the overlapping colors blend into white.
The region in an ascending conduit where magma breaks into particles carried by expanding gas; its depth varies.
Water stored beneath Earth's surface in soil and rock layers. It fills aquifers and feeds springs and underground streams.
Half of Earth. The Equator divides the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, which always have opposite seasons.
Pressure caused by the weight of the fluid above. In seawater it rises by about 1 atmosphere for every 10 m of depth.
Rock formed by the cooling and solidifying of molten materials.
How many times slower light travels in a material than in a vacuum. Water is about 1.33; a higher index means more bending.
The process by which water soaks into the soil and moves downward through soil layers. This water becomes groundwater.
Incoming solar radiation: how much sunlight energy reaches a surface, measured in watts per square meter (W/m²).
What happens when two waves overlap: where crests meet crests they add up and get stronger, and where crests meet troughs they cancel out.
Light bouncing off the inside surface of a material, like a ray reflecting off the back wall of a raindrop.
A flowing mixture of water and volcanic sediment.
Hot fluid or semifluid material below or within the earth's crust from which lava and other igneous rock is formed by cooling.
A subsurface region containing magma, crystals and gas.
Clumps of dead plankton, fecal pellets, mucus, and other organic bits that drift down from the surface and feed the deep sea.
A local region with more liquid melt within a crystal-rich magmatic system.
Rock that was once one form of rock but has changed to another under the influence of heat, pressure, or some other agent without passing through a liquid phase.
Slow cycles in Earth's tilt, wobble (precession), and orbit shape, lasting tens of thousands of years, that shift sunlight across the globe and help pace the ice ages.
The path one object follows around another because of gravity. Earth's orbit is a slightly oval ellipse that takes one year.
The point in an orbit where a planet is closest to the Sun. Earth reaches it around January 3, at about 147.1 million km.
Earth's closest point to the Sun (about January 3) and its farthest point (about July 4).
The upper layer of a body of water that gets enough sunlight for photosynthesis — roughly down to where 1% of surface light remains.
A bright star close to the point in the sky where Earth's axis points. Today it is Polaris; precession slowly changes it over thousands of years.
The slow wobble of Earth's axis, like a spinning top, that traces a circle in the sky about every 26,000 years and changes which star is the pole star.
Water that falls from clouds to Earth in the form of rain, snow, sleet, or hail. The process returns water to the surface.
A fast, ground-hugging mixture of hot volcanic gas and rock particles.
A comparison of two quantities by division, often written with a colon or as a fraction.
The bending of light as it passes from one material into another, such as from air into water, because light changes speed.
Rock that has formed through the deposition and solidification of sediment, especially sediment transported by water, ice, and wind.
A broad volcano with gentle slopes built mainly by fluid lava flows.
A sheet-shaped intrusion that runs approximately parallel to surrounding rock layers.
One of two moments each year (about June 21 and December 21) when one hemisphere leans most toward the Sun, giving it the longest day, and the other has its shortest day.
A volcano built from layers of lava and fragmented volcanic material.
The process by which snow or ice turns directly into water vapor, skipping the liquid phase entirely.
The spot on Earth where the Sun is straight overhead. It moves between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn over the year.
A faint pastel band just inside a rainbow's violet edge, caused by interference between light waves taking slightly different paths through the drop.
Rock fragments of any size ejected by a volcanic eruption.
A layer of water where temperature drops quickly with depth, separating warm surface water from the cold deep ocean.
Trimethylamine N-oxide, a small molecule deep-sea animals store to help their proteins keep working under high pressure. It also gives fish their “fishy” smell.
The process by which plants release water vapor from their leaves. Combined with evaporation, it's called evapotranspiration.
The latitude lines at 23.4°N (Cancer) and 23.4°S (Capricorn): the farthest north and south the Sun is ever straight overhead. Their latitude equals Earth's tilt.
Volcanic Explosivity Index: a scale describing explosive eruption size using ejecta volume and other evidence.
Resistance of a material to flow.
The invisible gas form of water. It floats in the atmosphere and becomes visible as clouds when it condenses.
The breaking down of rocks, soil, and minerals as well as wood and artificial materials through contact with the Earth's atmosphere, waters, and biological organisms.
The part of a machine that turns a control signal into action in the physical world, such as a motor, servo, speaker, or LED.
A precise sequence of steps for solving a problem or completing a task.

terms.definition: When a frequency above the Nyquist limit is sampled too slowly and shows up as a fake, lower frequency — like wagon wheels that seem to spin backward on film.
A mixture of two or more metals (or a metal and another element) combined to create a material with properties neither has alone, such as the tin-silver-copper mix used in lead-free solder.
Electric current that reverses direction many times a second, so its voltage keeps flipping polarity. Wall outlets in North America supply AC at 60 Hz.

A meter (or a multimeter's current mode) that measures electric current. It has very low resistance, so it must be placed in series so that the current flows through it, never across a voltage source.
The unit of electric current, written A. One amp is one coulomb of charge passing a point each second. Named after André-Marie Ampère.
The height of a wave — how far it swings from its resting middle line. For sound, bigger amplitude means louder.
The height of a wave: how far it swings from its middle value to its peak. For AC, the amplitude is the peak voltage.
A signal that can take any value in a range, like a voltage that slides smoothly from 0 V to 5 V. An Arduino reads it with analogRead() as a number from 0 to 1023.
A chip that measures a continuously changing voltage (like a microphone signal) many times a second and turns each measurement into a number a computer can store.
A circuit that measures a voltage and turns it into a number; on an Arduino UNO it maps 0–5 V to 0–1023, which analogRead() returns.
The terminal where conventional current enters a diode or LED: the positive side. On a new LED it is the longer leg; on the schematic symbol it is the flat side of the triangle.
A reactive robot planner where the goal attracts the robot and obstacles repel it, and the robot follows the combined force.
How quickly a compressor reacts once the signal rises above the threshold, usually measured in milliseconds.
An automatic volume control that turns a sound down when it gets louder than a set threshold, narrowing the gap between loud and quiet parts.
A compressor with a very high ratio and very fast attack that keeps a signal from ever exceeding a set ceiling.
A meter feature that picks the measurement range automatically and shows a prefix such as m, k, or M, so you must read the unit letters to know the value's size.
A robot that runs its own sense, think, act loop without a person making each decision.
How many signal symbols a serial link sends per second. At 9600 baud with 10 bits per byte, about 960 bytes travel each second.

terms.definition: How many signal symbols per second a serial link sends, such as 9600. Both ends must use the same baud rate or the text arrives as gibberish.
A number system with only two digits, 0 and 1. Each binary digit, or bit, can be stored as one LOW or HIGH voltage.
How many bits are used to store each sample of a digital signal. More bits give more levels to round to, so less quantization noise: 16-bit audio has 65,536 levels.
BLE: a short-range radio standard that sends small packets of data using very little power. Web pages can talk to BLE devices through Web Bluetooth.
The math of true and false, combined with NOT, AND, and OR, named for George Boole; it describes both logic gates and the && || ! operators in code.
A reusable prototyping board with a grid of push-fit sockets that lets components and jumper wires be connected and rearranged without soldering.
How much charge a capacitor stores for each volt across it, measured in farads (F). Real parts are usually microfarads (µF) or smaller.
A part that stores electric charge on two conducting plates separated by an insulator. It can release that charge quickly, smooth out bumpy voltage, or block DC while passing AC.
The tendency of a liquid to flow into narrow spaces without outside help, which is how solder wick draws up molten solder during desoldering.
The curve a chain or cable makes when it hangs freely under its own weight. Turned upside down, it is the shape of an arch that carries its load in pure compression.

The terminal where conventional current leaves a diode or LED: the negative side, marked by the bar on the symbol, the stripe on a diode, and the short leg and flat edge of an LED. In a vacuum tube it is the heated electrode that gives off electrons.
The 0-volt reference point of a circuit, usually the battery’s − side. Every voltage is measured from it, and every current path returns to it.
Every point joined by plain wire, which all share one voltage. On a breadboard, each connected row of five holes is one node.
Distortion that happens when a signal goes above the maximum level a system can handle, flattening the tops of the waveform.
When parts of a 3D scene disappear because they are closer or farther than the camera can draw, or when one object passes through another.
A steady square wave that tells a digital circuit when to take its next step; an Arduino UNO's clock ticks 16 million times a second (16 MHz).

Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor: chips that pair N-channel and P-channel MOSFETs in every gate so almost no current flows except while switching, which is why modern processors can run on batteries.
A number that multiplies a variable or quantity, such as 3 in 3x.
A joint where the solder never fully bonded because the metals were too cool, the flux was used up, or the joint moved while hardening. It looks dull, grainy, or lumpy and conducts unreliably.
An agreed set of rules for how two devices format, send, and answer messages, so each side understands the other.
How strongly a compressor reduces sound above the threshold; at 4:1, every 4 dB of input over the threshold comes out as 1 dB.
The bend in a compressor's transfer curve at the threshold; a soft knee eases compression in gradually, a hard knee starts it abruptly.
The level, in decibels, above which a compressor starts turning the sound down.
A material, like copper, whose electrons move easily, so current flows through it with little resistance.
The space of every possible pose of a robot, such as every combination of its joint angles. In it the whole robot is a single point, so motion planning becomes moving a point around obstacle regions.
An unbroken electrical path between two points, usually confirmed with a multimeter's continuity or beep test before trusting a joint.
The agreed direction for drawing current: out of the + terminal, through the circuit, and back to −. Electrons actually drift the other way, but every schematic symbol and arrow uses this convention.
A number in an ordered set that identifies a point’s position on a grid or in space.
A heavy weight that balances or drives a machine. In a trebuchet it is lifted high and its fall powers the throw.

terms.definition: A safety control that stops a machine automatically unless the operator keeps actively holding it or keeps sending signals.
Ignoring the rapid on-off flickers a mechanical switch makes for a few milliseconds when it is pressed, so one press counts as one press.
A logarithmic unit for comparing loudness or signal strength. Every +6 dB roughly doubles a wave’s amplitude; every +10 dB is about ten times the power.
A small capacitor, usually 100 nF, placed right next to a chip's power pin to supply sudden bursts of current so the supply voltage doesn't dip.
The number of independent ways a mechanism can move. Each robot joint adds one; placing a tool at any position and angle in 3-D space takes six.
How many turns ahead an AI calculates. A depth of 1 looks only at the immediate next move.

terms.definition: A robot drive with two independently powered wheels and no steering; it turns by spinning one wheel faster than the other.
A signal with only two states, HIGH or LOW (on or off, 1 or 0), such as a button that is either pressed or not.
A one-way valve for electric current. Current flows from anode to cathode and is blocked the other way, which makes diodes the parts used for rectification and reverse-polarity protection.

A multimeter mode that pushes about 1 mA through a part and displays the voltage across it. It shows a diode's or LED's forward voltage in one direction and OL in the other, revealing which lead is the anode.
Electric current that keeps flowing in one direction, so its voltage keeps one polarity. Batteries, solar cells, USB, and Arduino boards all use DC.
The percentage of each PWM cycle that the signal is on. 25% duty cycle is on a quarter of the time; 100% is always on.
The difference, in decibels, between the quietest and loudest parts of a sound or system.
DWA: a local planner that tests the speeds and turn rates a robot can reach in the next instant, predicts each arc, and picks the safest one heading toward the goal.
A property of particles that makes them push or pull on each other: like charges repel and opposite charges attract. Electrons are negative, protons positive. Measured in coulombs.
The flow of electric charge past a point each second, measured in amperes (A). Its symbol in equations is I.
A machine that turns electricity into spinning motion using the push between magnets and current-carrying coils. A generator run backward.
A can-shaped capacitor with large capacitance for its size that is polarized: the striped leg must go to the lower voltage, and it must never exceed its voltage rating.
Making a voltage in a wire by changing the magnetic field through it, by moving a magnet, moving the wire, or changing a current nearby. Generators and transformers work this way.
A tiny, negatively charged particle found around every atom. In a metal wire, loosely held electrons drift along to carry electric current.
Having a physical body that acts in the real world. A robot is embodied; a program that only changes information on a screen is not.
The tool at the end of a robot arm that does the work, such as a gripper, suction cup, welding torch, or paint sprayer.
The capacity to cause change or do work, such as moving, heating, or lighting something.

A dated record of a project's requirements, sketches, calculations, measurements, failures, and fixes, kept as you work so anyone can see how and why the design changed.
A set of audio filters that boost or cut chosen bands of frequencies, used to shape the tone of music or remove unwanted sounds like hum.
The unit of capacitance: one farad stores one coulomb of charge per volt. Real capacitors are usually measured in microfarads (µF), nanofarads (nF), or picofarads (pF).
A shortcut way of computing the Fourier transform (Cooley and Tukey, 1965) that is fast enough for computers to analyse sound, radio and images in real time.
A cycle where a system measures the result of what it just did and uses that measurement to decide what to do next, then repeats.
The smooth, concave cone of solder that forms between a pad and a component lead in a well-wetted joint.
An input pin connected to nothing that holds it at a voltage, so it drifts with static and stray signals and reads random values; a pull-up or pull-down resistor fixes it.
A chemical cleaning agent, often built into the core of solder wire, that removes oxide from metal surfaces so molten solder can bond to them.
A push or pull that can change an object’s motion or shape.

Describing a signal by which frequencies it contains and how strong each is — the spectrum, with amplitude on one axis and frequency on the other.

The branch of mathematics that studies shapes, sizes, positions, and spaces.

The curve a chain or cable makes when it hangs freely under its own weight. Turned upside down, it is the shape of an arch that carries its load in pure compression.
The glass picture tube in old TVs. It fires a beam of electrons at a glowing screen, sweeping it line by line to draw the picture.
A camera wired straight to a screen nearby, so the screen shows what the camera sees right now, with no broadcast in between.
The brain's habit of seeing an object's color as steady while the light changes, by estimating the color of the light and subtracting it.
One of the three kinds of color-sensing cells in the retina, tuned to long, medium or short wavelengths of light (roughly red, green and blue). Rods, the other type, work mainly in dim light.
Art made by tearing, peeling, or removing layers instead of gluing them on, such as a ripped poster that shows older posters underneath.
How far something sits from the camera or into the screen. In 3D software it is the Z direction, front to back.
A narrow stream of electrons. Because electrons carry charge, a magnet near the beam pushes it sideways and bends the picture.
A 1960s international group of artists, composers, and performers who staged playful, rule-breaking events and treated everyday actions as art.
Letting physics find a structure's shape, for example by hanging weighted chains or stretching fabric, instead of drawing the shape first and checking it afterwards.

The job a part does. The function of a structure in a living thing, a machine, or a design is what it is for and how it helps the whole work.
The branch of mathematics that studies shapes, sizes, positions, and spaces.
A picture of how two quantities are related, with one quantity on each axis and points or a line showing their values.
A testable explanation or prediction based on observations and prior knowledge.
An edge you see even though no edge is drawn there, because the brain connects separate fragments into a shape in front.
In hand-drawn animation, a drawing that goes between two key poses. Assistants drew the in-betweens after the lead animator drew the keys; their spacing sets how fast the movement feels.
Art built to fill a whole room or space, so viewers walk around or through it instead of looking at one object on a wall.
One of the few drawings or poses that tell the story of a movement, like Contact, Down, Passing, and Up in a walk. Everything else is in-between.
When a nerve cell that is active quiets its neighbors. It sharpens edges, which is why a border between light and dark looks more contrasty than it really is.
Thin bright and dark stripes you see where a smooth gradient meets a flat shade. They are not in the picture. Lateral inhibition is the classic explanation, though it does not explain every detail.
An animation camera that shoots down through several panes of glass art spaced at different distances, so near and far layers shift by different amounts and a flat painting gains depth.

The idea that color vision compares signals in opposing pairs: red versus green, blue versus yellow, and light versus dark. Tire one side of a pair and the other side wins, which gives opposite-colored afterimages.
The way a nearer object seems to shift against a farther background when your viewpoint moves. Close things appear to move more than distant ones.

The feeling of motion in a still picture made of repeating dark-to-light steps, strongest in the corner of the eye. Discovered by Fraser and Wilcox in 1979; Kitaoka's rotating snakes are the best-known example.

The old name for why quick still pictures look like motion: the eye and brain blend a fast series of slightly different images into smooth movement. Today it is explained mostly by the phi phenomenon and beta movement.
A point of view; in art, a method for showing depth and three-dimensional space on a flat surface.
An illusion of motion the brain creates when nearby lights or images switch on and off in quick succession, studied by psychologist Max Wertheimer in 1912.
Original evidence created during the time being studied, such as a letter, photograph, artifact, or firsthand account.
An early model built to test an idea, reveal problems, and guide improvements.
Creative works whose copyright has run out (or never existed). Anyone may copy, perform and change them.
A comparison of two quantities by division, often written with a colon or as a fraction.
The way a sense turns down its response to something steady, so it can notice changes instead. It is why you stop feeling your clothes and why afterimages happen.
The effect that makes the same gray or the same color look different depending on what surrounds it. A gray square looks lighter on black than on white.
A symbol or named value that can represent different numbers, measurements, or data.
Art that uses video and television (screens, cameras, recorded or live signals) as its material, instead of paint or stone.
A machine that colors, mixes, and distorts a video signal live, the way a music synthesizer shapes sound.
An assumption your brain makes before looking, such as 'light comes from above' or 'far things are smaller'. Priors make vision fast, and illusions are pictures where a prior gives the wrong answer.
A common song form of four sections: a main idea, its repeat, a contrasting bridge, and the main idea once more.
A note played louder than the notes around it.
A sharp (♯), flat (♭) or natural (♮) that changes a note by a half step.
A precise sequence of steps for solving a problem or completing a task.
When a frequency above the Nyquist limit is sampled too slowly and shows up as a fake, lower frequency — like wagon wheels that seem to spin backward on film.
The height of a wave — how far it swings from its resting middle line. For sound, bigger amplitude means louder.
A chip that measures a continuously changing voltage (like a microphone signal) many times a second and turns each measurement into a number a computer can store.
A note, often a half step above or below, that leads into a target note such as a chord tone.
The notes of a chord played one after another instead of all at once, the way a harp would play them.
The smallest unit of an element that still has that element’s chemical properties.
Hearing music in your mind when no sound is playing, for example by reading a score and imagining how it sounds.
A church mode’s high range, or its low range starting a fourth below.
An accent on beats 2 and 4, usually played on the snare.
A shape where one finger presses multiple strings, movable to any fret.
A strip of spruce glued lengthwise under a violin's top beneath the G-string foot of the bridge. It stiffens the top and helps carry low vibrations.
A repeating pattern of kick, snare and cymbal that a song is built on.
A slow loud-soft pulsing heard when two close frequencies interfere over time.
How many bits are used to store each sample of a digital signal. More bits give more levels to round to, so less quantization noise: 16-bit audio has 65,536 levels.
Hearing through the bones of the skull: vibration travels through bone straight to the inner ear, skipping the eardrum and middle ear.
The block at the hand end of a string player's bow. It holds the hair, slides when the screw is turned to tighten or loosen it, and is where the thumb rests.
The carved maple piece the strings pass over; it carries their vibration into the top.
One musician or group states a phrase and another answers it, like a conversation.
A piece in which one voice plays a melody and another copies it exactly, starting later, like singing a round.
A keyboard instrument whose hammers strike metal bars, giving a soft, bell-like sound. Tchaikovsky made it famous in The Nutcracker.
1/100 of an equal-tempered semitone. An octave is 1200 cents.
The scale degree that sets a modern mode apart from plain major or minor.
A shaped rest clamped to the lower edge of a violin or viola. The player's jaw rests on it so the instrument is held by the body, not the left hand.
A chord with a note other than the root on the bottom. First inversion puts the 3rd on the bottom; second inversion puts the 5th there.
A series of chords in a set order. Jazz musicians improvise over a repeating progression, which they call the “changes.”
A short name written above the melody, like G7 or Am, that tells the band which chord to play until the next symbol.
One of the notes that make up the chord sounding at that moment. C, E and G are the chord tones of C major.
Western music from about 1750 to 1820 (Haydn, Mozart, early Beethoven), prized for balance, clarity and elegant forms.
An early keyboard instrument in which each key presses a small brass blade (a tangent) against a string. Touch changes its loudness, but it is very quiet.
The symbol that tells you which pitches the lines and spaces mean: treble, bass or alto.
The symbol that tells you which pitches the staff's lines and spaces represent — treble (𝄞) for higher notes, bass (𝄢) for lower.
All chord tones stacked within a single octave.
The snail-shaped, fluid-filled part of the inner ear that turns vibration into nerve signals the brain hears as sound.
A note shared by two chords.
Short for accompanying: a pianist or guitarist playing chords in rhythm behind a melody or a soloist.
The notes as they actually sound, the way a piano plays them. Parts for transposing instruments are written in a different key from concert pitch.
A stable, pleasant-sounding interval, often tied to simple whole-number frequency ratios.
A new melody written over the chord progression of an existing song.
A bar of clicks before the groove starts, so you know the tempo.
The art of combining independent melodies so that each makes sense on its own and together they make good harmony.
A pair of strings tuned together and played as one, as on early guitars and today’s 12-string.
A felt pad that stops a string ringing when you release the key.
The right-hand piano pedal. It lifts the felt dampers off the strings, so notes keep ringing after the keys are released.
A logarithmic unit for comparing loudness or signal strength. Every +6 dB roughly doubles a wave’s amplitude; every +10 dB is about ten times the power.
Built from notes of the selected key.
Built from the notes of the selected key.
The small step of the enharmonic genus, about a quarter tone.
The chord built on the fifth note of a key (G major in the key of C). It creates tension that wants to resolve home to the tonic chord.
The difference, in decibels, between the quietest and loudest parts of a sound or system.
The capacity to cause change or do work, such as moving, heating, or lighting something.
Two spellings of the same sound, like C♯ and D♭.
A tuning system that divides the octave into twelve equal frequency ratios of 2^(1/12).
A tuning that divides the octave into 12 equal semitones.
A set of audio filters that boost or cut chosen bands of frequencies, used to shape the tone of music or remove unwanted sounds like hum.
In a piano, the part of the action that lets the hammer fly free and fall back the instant it strikes the string, so the string can keep ringing.
The character or moral effect a type of music was believed to have.
The two f-shaped openings in the top of a violin-family instrument. They let the top flex and let air move in and out of the body.
A collection of lead sheets. Musicians “fake” (make up) the accompaniment from the chord symbols instead of reading every note.
Thin wooden strips glued under a classical guitar's top in a fan shape, keeping the top strong while leaving it free to vibrate.
A shortcut way of computing the Fourier transform (Cooley and Tukey, 1965) that is fast enough for computers to analyse sound, radio and images in real time.
A short break that signals a change is coming, usually ending in a crash.
The note a chant ends on, which identifies its church mode.
A small screw lever on the tailpiece for small pitch changes.
1 = thumb, 5 = pinky, for both hands.
A push or pull that can change an object’s motion or shape.
The early piano of the 1700s and early 1800s, with a wooden frame, leather-covered hammers, and a lighter sound than a modern piano. Its name means “loud-soft.”
Breaking a complex wave into a sum of simple sine wave components.
Describing a signal by which frequencies it contains and how strong each is — the spectrum, with amplitude on one axis and frequency on the other.
The block at the end of the bow that holds the hair and is moved by the screw.
A piece in which a short theme enters in one voice after another, then is developed, imitated and combined with itself.
The job a part does. The function of a structure in a living thing, a machine, or a design is what it is for and how it helps the whole work.
The lowest frequency in a musical sound — the rate at which the whole wave pattern repeats. It sets the pitch you hear.
How the movable notes divide the fourth: diatonic, chromatic, or enharmonic (pl. genera).
The branch of mathematics that studies shapes, sizes, positions, and spaces.
A note played very quietly, felt more than heard.
A magnet wrapped in thousands of turns of copper wire. A vibrating steel string disturbs its magnetic field and makes a small electric signal that an amplifier can make loud.
An early Greek tuning or style named for a people or region (pl. harmoniai).
A sine-wave component of a sound at a whole-number multiple (2×, 3×, 4×…) of the fundamental frequency. The mix of harmonics gives an instrument its timbre.
The family of frequencies (f, 2f, 3f...) a fixed-length vibrator can sustain.
A keyboard instrument whose strings are plucked by small quills when you press the keys. It is bright and clear, but every note sounds at the same loudness however you press.
A filter that lets frequencies above its cutoff through and turns down everything below it. Used to remove rumble and hum.
What happens when two waves overlap: where crests meet crests they add up and get stronger, and where crests meet troughs they cancel out.
The distance between two notes, named by number and quality.
The distance between two notes: count letter names for its number and semitones for its quality.
The semitone distance between two notes.
How accurately a played or sung note matches the pitch it is meant to be.
A chord played with a note other than the root as the lowest note.
A chord with a chord tone other than the root as its lowest sounding note.
A chord with a note other than the root on the bottom.
A chord with a note other than the root on the bottom.
The tune turned upside down.
A note’s place in the key’s scale, counted from the tonic.
A note’s place in the scale, counted from the tonic.
The sharps or flats at the start of the staff that apply to the whole piece.
A page of music with just the melody on one staff and chord symbols above it; each player makes up their own part from the chords.
A short extra line added above or below the staff for a note that goes past it.
A short extra line for notes above or below the staff.
A filter that lets frequencies below its cutoff through and turns down everything above it. Used to remove hiss and to stop aliasing before sampling.
A craftsperson who builds and repairs stringed instruments such as violins and guitars.
Turning a melody upside down: every move up becomes the same-sized move down, mirrored around a starting note.
Two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds as a single unit.
A plan for how a piece is performed: who plays which part, when each instrument enters, and how the parts fit together.
How many layers of sound happen at once and how they relate: one melody alone, a melody with accompaniment, or several independent lines.
A point on a standing wave or vibrating surface that stays still while the parts around it move.
A single point in a graph or tree, like one cell on a map, one city on a route, or one board state in a game tree.
A filter that removes one narrow band of frequencies, such as 60 Hz electrical hum, while leaving the rest of the sound almost untouched.
Half the sampling rate — the highest frequency a sampled system can capture correctly. Anything above it gets aliased.
The 12-semitone span between one note and the next with the same name.
One of seven octave-long windows in the Greek system, each with its own order of steps.
A chord that uses at least one unfretted string.
A round-backed, short-necked string instrument with no frets, played across the Middle East and North Africa. Brought to Spain in the Middle Ages, it became the ancestor of the European lute.
Laying a piano's long bass strings diagonally over the other strings, so they fit in the case and drive the middle of the soundboard.
The interval of seven half steps, such as G up to D. Neighbouring violin strings are tuned a perfect fifth apart.
How a musician shapes a melody in time: where each phrase starts and ends, which notes it leans on, and where it breathes.
A paper roll punched with holes that makes a player piano play by itself. A roll can capture a pianist’s notes and timing.
A magnet wrapped in wire that turns a vibrating steel string into an electric signal.
Notes before the first full bar.
One or more notes before the first full bar of a tune, leading into the first strong beat. Also called an anacrusis.
Instrumental music that tells a story or paints a scene, such as birdsong or a storm, without using words.
Creative works whose copyright has run out (or never existed). Anyone may copy, perform and change them.
The gap of about 23.5 cents between 12 pure fifths and 7 octaves.
Perfect, major, minor, augmented or diminished.
Rounding each measured sample to the nearest allowed level when a signal is digitised. The rounding errors are heard as a faint hiss called quantization noise.
American piano music popular from about 1895 to 1920, with a steady, march-like left hand under a syncopated right-hand melody.
A comparison of two quantities by division, often written with a colon or as a fraction.
The note psalm verses are chanted on in a given mode (also called the tenor).
Large-amplitude response when a driving frequency matches a system's natural frequency.
An acoustic guitar with thin metal cones inside that act like loudspeakers, making it louder and brighter than a wooden guitar. Invented in the 1920s.
In music, playing a melody backwards, from its last note to its first.
A pattern of sounds and silences organized through time.
In a Baroque concerto, the passage the full orchestra plays at the start and brings back between the soloist’s sections. Italian for “little return.”
Western music from about 1820 to 1900 (Chopin, Tchaikovsky), which put personal feeling, drama and bigger orchestras first.
A musical form in which a main theme keeps coming back between contrasting sections: A B A C A.
The note a chord is named after.
Hardened tree resin rubbed on bow hair so it grips the string and makes it vibrate.
Stretching and pushing the tempo for expression: taking time in one place and making it up in another. Italian for “robbed.”
A short, named sticking pattern practiced to build control and speed.
How many measurements (samples) per second a digital system takes of a signal. CD audio uses 44,100 samples per second.
A set of notes in order, climbing by a pattern of whole and half steps.
Improvised jazz singing with wordless syllables, as if the voice were an instrument.
A three-note chord of just the root, 3rd and 7th: the notes that tell you what kind of chord it is. A favorite of bebop pianists.
Notation like C/E — a C chord with E in the bass.
Do Re Mi Fa Sol La Ti: syllables for the notes of a scale.
An electric guitar with a solid wooden body instead of a hollow one, so it can be played very loud without howling feedback.
A Classical plan for a movement: an exposition that presents two themes, a development that transforms them, and a recapitulation that brings them back home.
A large, thin wooden board in a piano or other string instrument that picks up the strings' vibrations and moves the air, making them loud enough to hear.
A thin spruce dowel standing inside a violin between the top and back, near the E-string foot of the bridge. It is held by pressure, not glue, and shapes the instrument's tone.
A chart of a signal’s ingredients: each frequency it contains and how much of it there is.
Five lines and four spaces where notes live.

Which hand (R or L) plays each note.
A pair (sometimes a trio) of strings tuned together and played as if they were one string, as on early guitars, lutes, and today's 12-string guitar.
An uneven, long–short feel applied to eighth notes.
Eighth notes played long-short.

Putting notes or accents off the beat, so the music pushes against the steady pulse.
The speed of a piece of music, usually measured in beats per minute.
Sudden changes between loud and soft levels, like steps, instead of gradual swells. Typical of Baroque music.
Four notes spanning a perfect fourth, with two fixed outer notes and two movable inner notes.
The "colour" or character of a sound that lets you tell a flute from a violin playing the same note at the same loudness. It comes from the mix of harmonics.
Describing a signal by how it changes over time — the waveform you would see on an oscilloscope, with amplitude on one axis and time on the other.
Ringing, buzzing or whistling in the ears that no outside sound is causing. Beethoven described it in his letters.
A Greek transposition key. It is often confused with the species.
Taking turns improvising four bars at a time with another player, often the drummer.
Move a whole tune into a different key.

A three-note chord built from stacked thirds.
A three-note chord: root, 3rd, and 5th.
